title: Green Nanotechnology-Based Zinc Oxide (ZnO) Nanomaterials for Biomedical Applications: A Comprehensive Review

subsections.section_title: Principles and Mechanisms of Green Synthesis of ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.content:
Plant extract-mediated synthesis of ZnO nanomaterials leverages the phytochemicals present in leaves, fruits, roots, and flowers as natural reducing and capping agents, offering a sustainable alternative to conventional chemical methods. Polyphenols, flavonoids, terpenoids, and alkaloids in plant extracts facilitate the reduction of zinc precursors (e.g., Zn(NO₃)₂ or ZnAc₂) and stabilize the resulting nanoparticles, preventing aggregation and controlling size and shape. This method operates under mild conditions—often at ambient temperature and pressure—significantly reducing energy consumption and eliminating toxic solvents. The diversity of plant sources allows for tunable morphologies, including spheres, rods, and hexagonal structures, depending on the extract composition and reaction parameters.

For instance, aqueous extracts of Aloe vera, Ocimum sanctum, and Citrus limon have been shown to produce monodisperse ZnO nanoparticles with sizes ranging from 10 to 50 nm, as confirmed by TEM and XRD analyses [1]. Similarly, Moringa oleifera leaf extract has demonstrated dual functionality in reduction and stabilization, yielding ZnO with enhanced photocatalytic activity [2]. The role of specific biomolecules, such as quercetin in onion peel extract, has been correlated with the formation of anisotropic ZnO nanostructures [3]. These biosynthesized nanoparticles exhibit improved biocompatibility and reduced cytotoxicity, making them suitable for biomedical and environmental applications.

subsections.section_title: Principles and Mechanisms of Green Synthesis of ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.content:
Microbial synthesis of ZnO nanomaterials leverages the metabolic activity of bacteria and fungi to reduce zinc ions into zinc oxide nanoparticles under ambient conditions, offering a sustainable alternative to physicochemical methods. Bacterial strains such as Bacillus subtilis and Pseudomonas aeruginosa have demonstrated efficient intracellular and extracellular synthesis of ZnO nanoparticles, with cell wall components and secreted enzymes facilitating nucleation and stabilization [1]. Fungal species, including Fusarium oxysporum and Aspergillus niger, exhibit superior extracellular synthesis capabilities due to their extensive hyphal networks and high secretion of reductive metabolites like proteins and organic acids, enabling precise control over particle size and morphology [2]. The bio-reduction process is often mediated by NADH-dependent reductases and zinc-binding peptides, which not only reduce Zn²⁺ but also prevent aggregation through capping action [3]. This biological templating results in uniform, crystalline ZnO nanoparticles with narrow size distributions, often in the range of 10–50 nm, suitable for biomedical and catalytic applications.

Compared to plant extract-based methods, microbial synthesis offers enhanced reproducibility and scalability through controlled fermentation, while avoiding the compositional variability inherent in botanical sources. Moreover, fungal systems have shown higher tolerance to metal toxicity, enabling synthesis at elevated zinc concentrations without loss of viability [4]. Recent studies have further demonstrated the functionalization of microbially synthesized ZnO with antimicrobial and photocatalytic properties, validating their potential for environmental remediation and wound healing applications [5].

subsections.section_title: Principles and Mechanisms of Green Synthesis of ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.content:
Biopolymer-assisted synthesis of ZnO nanomaterials leverages naturally derived polymers such as chitosan, starch, cellulose, and alginate to act as both reducing and capping agents, enabling precise control over nanoparticle size, shape, and dispersion. These biopolymers contain functional groups (e.g., -NH₂, -OH) that coordinate with zinc ions, facilitating nucleation and inhibiting uncontrolled growth. Chitosan, in particular, has been widely employed due to its biocompatibility, film-forming ability, and inherent antimicrobial properties, resulting in ZnO nanoparticles with enhanced stability and bioactivity. For instance, chitosan-stabilized ZnO nanoparticles demonstrated improved photocatalytic efficiency and reduced aggregation compared to conventionally synthesized counterparts [1].

Starch and cellulose derivatives have also been utilized to synthesize ZnO nanoparticles under mild conditions, with the polysaccharide matrix providing a templating effect that yields uniform morphologies. Alginate-based systems further enable encapsulation and controlled release applications, particularly in biomedical contexts. These biopolymer matrices not only replace toxic surfactants but also impart additional functionalities such as mucoadhesion and biodegradability, expanding the utility of ZnO in drug delivery and wound healing [2].

The integration of biopolymers with green synthesis protocols significantly reduces environmental impact by eliminating hazardous solvents and high-energy inputs. Moreover, the resulting nanocomposites often exhibit synergistic effects, combining the antimicrobial properties of ZnO with the bioactive nature of the polymer scaffold [3].

subsections.section_title: Principles and Mechanisms of Green Synthesis of ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.content:
Green synthesis of ZnO nanomaterials offers distinct advantages over conventional chemical and physical methods, particularly in terms of environmental sustainability and energy efficiency. Traditional approaches such as sol-gel, hydrothermal, and chemical precipitation often rely on toxic precursors, high temperatures, and hazardous solvents, contributing to significant ecological and health risks [1]. In contrast, green methods utilize biogenic reducing and capping agents derived from plants, microbes, or biopolymers, enabling synthesis at ambient or mild conditions with minimal waste generation [2].

Furthermore, green synthesis typically yields nanoparticles with improved biocompatibility and surface functionality due to the natural capping agents, which can eliminate the need for additional surface modification steps required in conventional methods [3]. Studies have demonstrated that ZnO nanoparticles synthesized via green routes exhibit comparable or superior photocatalytic and antimicrobial performance to those produced by chemical methods, while avoiding the use of strong reducing agents like sodium borohydride or hydrazine [4].

Economic analyses also indicate that green synthesis can reduce production costs by eliminating expensive equipment and energy-intensive processes, although scalability remains a challenge [5]. Nevertheless, the integration of green synthesis with industrial processes is gaining momentum due to regulatory pressures and consumer demand for eco-friendly nanomaterials [6].

subsections.section_title: Physicochemical Properties and Characterization of Green-Synthesized ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.content:
The morphology and size distribution of green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles are critically influenced by the choice of biological reducing and capping agents, as well as synthesis conditions such as pH, temperature, and reaction time. Plant extracts, for instance, often yield spherical or hexagonal nanoparticles with sizes ranging from 10 to 80 nm, depending on the phytochemical composition of the extract. Studies using Aloe vera leaf extract have demonstrated the formation of predominantly spherical particles with an average size of 25–40 nm, attributed to the stabilizing role of flavonoids and phenolic compounds ref [10]. Similarly, fungal-mediated synthesis using Aspergillus niger has produced irregularly shaped nanoparticles with broader size distributions (30–100 nm), reflecting the complex extracellular protein and enzyme milieu involved in nucleation and growth ref [8]. Bacterial biosynthesis, particularly with Bacillus subtilis, tends to yield more uniform, crystalline nanoparticles (20–50 nm) due to controlled enzymatic reduction and surface capping ref [7]. The use of polysaccharide-rich biomolecules, such as chitosan or alginate, further modulates particle aggregation and size, often resulting in narrower size distributions and enhanced colloidal stability ref [11].

Advanced imaging techniques, including TEM and SEM, combined with dynamic light scattering (DLS), are essential for accurate morphological and size characterization. Variability in size distribution is frequently linked to the concentration of metal precursors and incubation duration, with prolonged reaction times often leading to Ostwald ripening and particle growth. These structural features directly impact biological interactions and functional efficacy in biomedical applications, underscoring the need for precise control over biosynthesis parameters.

subsections.section_title: Physicochemical Properties and Characterization of Green-Synthesized ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.content:
The crystallinity and phase purity of green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles are critical determinants of their functional performance in biomedical and photocatalytic applications. X-ray diffraction (XRD) is the most widely employed technique to assess crystalline structure, with most biosynthesized ZnO nanoparticles exhibiting a hexagonal wurtzite phase, consistent with standard JCPDS card no. 36-1451. High crystallinity is often achieved through optimized biosynthesis conditions, such as controlled pH, temperature, and incubation time, which facilitate orderly ion nucleation and growth. For instance, fungal-mediated synthesis using Fusarium oxysporum yielded highly crystalline ZnO with minimal amorphous content, as confirmed by sharp diffraction peaks and low full-width at half-maximum (FWHM) values [1]. Similarly, plant extract-mediated synthesis using Ocimum sanctum resulted in phase-pure ZnO without secondary oxide impurities, as verified by the absence of extraneous peaks in XRD patterns [2].

The absence of secondary phases, such as Zn(OH)₂ or ZnCO₃, is often attributed to the reducing and capping agents in biological extracts that promote direct Zn²⁺ reduction to ZnO rather than intermediate hydroxide formation. Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) and Raman spectroscopy further corroborate phase purity by identifying characteristic vibrational modes of wurtzite ZnO, such as the E₂(high) mode at ~437 cm⁻¹, while excluding signatures of impurities [3]. High-resolution transmission electron microscopy (HRTEM) with selected area electron diffraction (SAED) provides complementary evidence of single-crystalline domains with lattice fringes matching the (100), (002), and (101) planes of wurtzite ZnO [4].

subsections.section_title: Physicochemical Properties and Characterization of Green-Synthesized ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.content:
The surface chemistry of green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles is predominantly governed by biomolecules from the plant or microbial extract used in synthesis, which act as capping and stabilizing agents. These include polyphenols, flavonoids, terpenoids, proteins, and organic acids that adsorb onto the nanoparticle surface, forming a bioorganic corona. This corona not only prevents aggregation but also imparts functional groups such as hydroxyl, carbonyl, and carboxyl moieties, which enhance colloidal stability and biocompatibility. Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy consistently reveals characteristic peaks corresponding to these functional groups, confirming their role in nucleation and growth modulation.

The nature of the biomolecular capping layer directly influences surface charge, hydrophilicity, and reactivity, which are critical for biomedical interactions. For instance, ZnO nanoparticles synthesized using Camellia sinensis extract exhibit enhanced surface carboxyl groups, facilitating improved cellular uptake and reduced cytotoxicity compared to chemically synthesized counterparts. Similarly, fungal-mediated synthesis yields surface-bound proteins and polysaccharides that confer antifouling properties and prolonged circulation in biological media. These surface modifications are not merely passive coatings but actively participate in bio-nano interactions, as demonstrated by their role in targeted drug delivery and antimicrobial efficacy.

Advanced surface analysis techniques such as X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) and zeta potential measurements further validate the presence and density of functional groups, enabling correlation between biosynthesis conditions and surface properties. The variability in extract composition across plant sources leads to distinct surface chemistries, underscoring the need for standardized characterization protocols to ensure reproducibility in biomedical applications.

subsections.section_title: Physicochemical Properties and Characterization of Green-Synthesized ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.content:
Green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles exhibit tunable optical properties dictated by biosynthesis conditions, including plant extract composition, pH, temperature, and reaction duration. These nanoparticles typically display a strong UV absorption edge near 370–380 nm, corresponding to the bandgap of wurtzite ZnO, with slight blue shifts observed due to quantum confinement effects in smaller particles. Photoluminescence spectra often reveal a near-band-edge emission in the ultraviolet region and a broad visible emission band attributed to oxygen vacancies and surface defects, which can be modulated by phytochemical capping agents that alter defect density and surface passivation. The electronic band structure is further influenced by the presence of organic biomolecules on the surface, which can introduce mid-gap states and affect charge carrier recombination dynamics.

Studies have demonstrated that ZnO nanoparticles synthesized using Moringa oleifera extract exhibit enhanced photoluminescence quantum yield compared to chemically synthesized counterparts, attributed to improved crystallinity and reduced non-radiative recombination pathways [1]. Similarly, fungal-mediated synthesis using Aspergillus niger yields ZnO with suppressed defect-related visible emission, suggesting controlled oxygen vacancy formation during bioreduction [2]. The photocatalytic activity of green-synthesized ZnO under visible light is often enhanced by surface-bound phenolic compounds that extend light absorption via sensitization, as shown in studies using Camellia sinensis and quercetin-based syntheses [3][4]. These optical and electronic modifications directly impact their efficacy in biomedical applications such as photodynamic therapy and biosensing.

subsections.section_title: Biocompatibility and Toxicological Profiles of Green ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.content:
In vitro cytotoxicity studies of green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles consistently demonstrate reduced cellular toxicity compared to their chemically synthesized counterparts, primarily attributed to bio-capping agents that modulate surface reactivity and ion release kinetics. Studies using human keratinocyte (HaCaT) and lung epithelial (A549) cell lines show that plant extract-capped ZnO nanoparticles exhibit higher cell viability at equivalent concentrations, with IC50 values 1.5- to 3-fold higher than those of chemically synthesized ZnO. For instance, ZnO nanoparticles synthesized using Camellia sinensis extract displayed significantly lower ROS generation and mitochondrial dysfunction in A549 cells, correlating with upregulated antioxidant enzyme expression ref [15]. Similarly, Bacillus subtilis-mediated ZnO nanoparticles induced minimal membrane damage and caspase-3 activation in fibroblast (L929) cells, even at doses where chemically synthesized ZnO caused substantial apoptosis ref [5].

The role of phytochemical capping in mitigating cytotoxicity is further evidenced by studies using Aloe vera-capped ZnO, which showed reduced lysosomal stress and preserved lysosomal membrane integrity in human dermal fibroblasts compared to polyethylene glycol-stabilized ZnO ref [7]. Dose-response analyses across multiple cell lines confirm that green-synthesized ZnO maintains biocompatibility up to 50–100 μg/mL, whereas conventional ZnO often triggers toxicity below 25 μg/mL. These findings underscore the protective influence of natural capping agents in modulating nanoparticle-cell interactions and limiting Zn²⁺ ion burst release, a key driver of oxidative stress and cytotoxicity.

subsections.section_title: Biocompatibility and Toxicological Profiles of Green ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.content:
In vivo biocompatibility studies of green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles have demonstrated significantly reduced systemic toxicity compared to chemically synthesized counterparts, primarily due to the stabilizing and bioactive nature of phytochemical or microbial capping agents. In murine models, ZnO nanoparticles synthesized using Ocimum sanctum leaf extract showed no significant alterations in liver or kidney function markers at therapeutic doses, with histopathological analyses revealing intact tissue architecture over 14 days post-administration ref [22]. Similarly, ZnO nanoparticles capped with Curcuma longa rhizome extract exhibited minimal inflammatory response in rat lung tissue following intratracheal instillation, with lower levels of TNF-α and IL-6 compared to citrate-stabilized ZnO ref [23]. A study in zebrafish embryos exposed to biosynthesized ZnO via aqueous immersion reported higher survival rates and reduced developmental abnormalities than those exposed to chemically synthesized nanoparticles, attributing the enhanced safety to the presence of polyphenolic capping ligands that mitigate oxidative stress ref [24].

Long-term biodistribution studies in mice indicate that green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles are efficiently cleared via hepatic and renal pathways, with no persistent accumulation in vital organs beyond 28 days ref [25]. Furthermore, immunohistochemical analyses of spleen and lymph node tissues from rats administered green ZnO revealed no signs of lymphocytic infiltration or granuloma formation, suggesting absence of chronic immune activation ref [26]. These findings collectively underscore the potential of bio-capped ZnO for safe biomedical applications, provided synthesis parameters and dosing regimens are carefully controlled.

subsections.section_title: Biocompatibility and Toxicological Profiles of Green ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.subsection_title: Role of bio-capping in reducing toxicity
subsections.content:
Bio-capping in green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles plays a pivotal role in mitigating toxicity by modulating surface chemistry, reducing reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, and preventing direct ion leaching. Phytochemicals and biomolecules such as polyphenols, flavonoids, and proteins adsorbed onto the nanoparticle surface during biosynthesis form a biocompatible shield that limits Zn²⁺ dissolution, a primary driver of cytotoxicity. This capping layer also enhances colloidal stability, reducing nonspecific cellular interactions and subsequent inflammatory responses. Studies have demonstrated that bio-capped ZnO nanoparticles exhibit significantly lower ROS induction in mammalian cells compared to chemically synthesized counterparts, attributed to the antioxidant properties of the capping agents ref [21].

Protein-mediated capping, as observed in Trichoderma harzianum-synthesized ZnO, not only stabilizes the nanoparticles but also imparts bio-recognition properties that facilitate controlled cellular uptake and reduce lysosomal stress ref [19]. Similarly, polysaccharide-based capping from Aloe vera or chitosan has been shown to attenuate membrane disruption and mitochondrial dysfunction in epithelial and immune cells ref [9]. The presence of reducing and stabilizing biomolecules also alters surface charge and hydrophilicity, minimizing opsonization and enhancing biocompatibility in vivo ref [14].

subsections.section_title: Biocompatibility and Toxicological Profiles of Green ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.subsection_title: Comparative toxicity: green vs. chemically synthesized ZnO
subsections.content:
Green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles consistently demonstrate reduced cytotoxicity compared to their chemically synthesized counterparts across multiple in vitro and in vivo models. The bio-capping agents derived from plant extracts or microbial metabolites mitigate oxidative stress and membrane damage by stabilizing particle surfaces and limiting uncontrolled Zn²⁺ ion release. For instance, ZnO nanoparticles synthesized using Curcuma longa extract exhibited significantly lower ROS generation and higher cell viability in human keratinocytes than chemically synthesized ZnO, attributed to the antioxidant properties of curcuminoids ref [18]. Similarly, zebrafish embryos exposed to biosynthesized ZnO showed reduced developmental abnormalities and mortality rates compared to those exposed to chemically synthesized particles, highlighting the protective role of phytochemical capping ref [26].

Comparative studies further reveal that chemically synthesized ZnO induces higher levels of inflammatory cytokines and mitochondrial dysfunction in macrophages, whereas green-synthesized variants elicit milder immune responses due to their more biocompatible surface chemistry ref [16]. In murine models, green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles demonstrated improved tissue clearance and reduced hepatic and renal accumulation, suggesting enhanced biodegradability and lower long-term toxicity ref [21]. These findings underscore that the synthesis route, not merely the chemical composition, critically determines biological outcomes.

subsections.section_title: Antimicrobial and Anticancer Applications of Green ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.content:
Green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles exhibit potent antibacterial activity against both Gram-positive and Gram-negative pathogens, including Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. The antimicrobial efficacy is primarily attributed to the generation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which induce oxidative stress, lipid peroxidation, and DNA damage in microbial cells. Additionally, direct contact between ZnO nanoparticles and bacterial membranes leads to structural disruption, increased permeability, and leakage of intracellular contents. Studies have demonstrated that phytochemically capped ZnO nanoparticles synthesized using Ocimum sanctum leaf extract significantly inhibit biofilm formation in clinical isolates of multidrug-resistant bacteria, outperforming conventional antibiotics in some cases.

Antifungal activity against pathogenic fungi such as Candida albicans, Aspergillus fumigatus, and Fusarium oxysporum has also been consistently reported. The mechanism involves disruption of fungal cell walls and membranes, coupled with intracellular ROS accumulation that impairs mitochondrial function and metabolic activity. Green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles using Citrus limon peel extract have shown superior antifungal efficacy compared to chemically synthesized counterparts, attributed to enhanced surface reactivity and phytochemical synergy. The selectivity of these nanoparticles toward microbial cells over mammalian cells is further enhanced by the biocompatible capping agents derived from plant extracts, which modulate surface charge and reduce nonspecific toxicity.

subsections.section_title: Antimicrobial and Anticancer Applications of Green ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.content:
Green-synthesized zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO NPs) have demonstrated promising antiviral activity against a range of enveloped and non-enveloped viruses, primarily through mechanisms involving reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, viral envelope disruption, and inhibition of viral entry or replication. Studies have shown that plant-mediated ZnO NPs can effectively inactivate influenza A virus by damaging the viral lipid envelope and suppressing hemagglutinin activity, thereby preventing host cell attachment. Similarly, ZnO NPs synthesized using Moringa oleifera extract have exhibited significant inhibitory effects against herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) by interfering with viral DNA replication and reducing plaque formation in vitro.

Recent evidence indicates that ZnO NPs capped with phytochemicals from Curcuma longa and Azadirachta indica can suppress human papillomavirus (HPV) replication by modulating cellular signaling pathways involved in viral oncogenesis. Furthermore, green-synthesized ZnO NPs have shown potential in blocking SARS-CoV-2 pseudovirus entry into ACE2-expressing cells, likely through interaction with spike protein domains and disruption of membrane integrity. The biocompatible capping agents in biosynthesized NPs enhance stability and reduce cytotoxicity, allowing for selective antiviral action without significant host cell damage.

subsections.section_title: Antimicrobial and Anticancer Applications of Green ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.content:
Green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles exert anticancer effects primarily through the induction of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which disrupt cellular redox homeostasis and trigger oxidative stress-mediated apoptosis in malignant cells. The phytochemical capping agents used in biosynthesis enhance the stability and cellular uptake of these nanoparticles, facilitating intracellular Zn²⁺ ion release that further amplifies mitochondrial dysfunction and caspase activation. Studies have demonstrated selective cytotoxicity toward cancer cells over normal cells, attributed to the higher basal ROS levels and altered metabolism in tumor cells, making them more vulnerable to additional oxidative insult. Additionally, ZnO nanoparticles can induce DNA damage and cell cycle arrest, particularly at the G2/M phase, through modulation of p53 and cyclin-dependent kinase pathways.

Membrane disruption is another key mechanism, where the surface charge and nanoscale topography of green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles promote direct interaction with the negatively charged phospholipid bilayers of cancer cells, leading to loss of membrane integrity and necrotic cell death. Synergistic effects are observed when phytochemical capping agents, such as flavonoids or polyphenols, possess intrinsic pro-apoptotic properties, thereby enhancing the overall therapeutic efficacy. Recent evidence also suggests that these nanoparticles can inhibit metastasis by downregulating matrix metalloproteinases and suppressing epithelial-mesenchymal transition markers.

subsections.section_title: Antimicrobial and Anticancer Applications of Green ZnO Nanomaterials
subsections.content:
Selective targeting of cancer cells by green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles is facilitated by their surface phytochemical capping, which enhances affinity for overexpressed receptors on malignant cells while sparing normal tissues. For instance, Azadirachta indica-capped ZnO nanoparticles demonstrated preferential uptake in cervical cancer cells via folate receptor-mediated endocytosis, minimizing toxicity to non-cancerous epithelial cells ref [21]. Similarly, quercetin-capped ZnO nanoparticles exhibited enhanced selectivity toward breast cancer lines due to the antioxidant–prooxidant duality of quercetin, which amplifies ROS stress selectively in metabolically hyperactive tumor cells ref [17].

Combination therapies leveraging green ZnO nanoparticles have shown synergistic efficacy with conventional chemotherapeutics and photodynamic agents. Co-administration of biosynthesized ZnO with doxorubicin significantly enhanced apoptosis in multidrug-resistant ovarian cancer cells by overcoming P-glycoprotein efflux, as demonstrated in vitro ref [17]. Furthermore, when paired with low-dose UV irradiation, green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles amplified photodynamic therapy outcomes in melanoma models by boosting intracellular ROS beyond the threshold for necroptosis, while reducing systemic toxicity compared to free photosensitizers ref [17]. These strategies highlight the potential of green ZnO as a multifunctional adjuvant in precision oncology.

subsections.section_title: Wound Healing, Drug Delivery, and Tissue Engineering Applications
subsections.content:
Green-synthesized zinc oxide (ZnO) nanoparticles have emerged as promising candidates for advanced wound dressings due to their intrinsic antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and pro-regenerative properties. When incorporated into hydrogel or fibrous matrices, these nanoparticles enhance moisture retention while simultaneously inhibiting bacterial colonization, thereby creating an optimal microenvironment for re-epithelialization. Studies demonstrate that phytochemically capped ZnO nanoparticles significantly accelerate wound closure in murine models by modulating pro-inflammatory cytokines and promoting fibroblast proliferation, with reduced scar formation compared to conventional dressings.

Furthermore, green ZnO nanoparticles stimulate angiogenesis through upregulation of VEGF and HIF-1α in dermal cells, facilitating vascular network formation essential for tissue regeneration. Their antioxidant capacity, derived from surface-bound phytochemicals, mitigates oxidative stress at the wound site, preserving extracellular matrix integrity. Recent work has shown that ZnO nanoparticles synthesized using Aloe vera extract, when embedded in chitosan-based films, exhibit sustained zinc ion release and superior biocompatibility, leading to faster epithelial migration and collagen deposition in full-thickness skin wounds.

subsections.section_title: Wound Healing, Drug Delivery, and Tissue Engineering Applications
subsections.content:
Green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles have emerged as promising nanocarriers for controlled drug and gene delivery due to their tunable surface chemistry, biocompatibility, and pH-responsive degradation. Phytochemical capping agents not only stabilize the nanoparticles but also enable functionalization with therapeutic payloads, facilitating targeted release at pathological sites. For instance, ZnO nanoparticles synthesized using Moringa oleifera extract demonstrated sustained release of ibuprofen and enhanced cellular uptake in inflamed tissues, leveraging the natural ligands for improved bioadhesion. Similarly, curcumin-loaded ZnO nanoparticles, capped with Camellia sinensis polyphenols, exhibited controlled release kinetics and synergistic anti-inflammatory effects in vitro, surpassing free drug efficacy.

In gene delivery, green ZnO nanoparticles have been engineered to complex with plasmid DNA or siRNA, exploiting their positive surface charge for electrostatic binding. Studies have shown that ZnO nanoparticles synthesized via Trichoderma harzianum-mediated protein capping effectively delivered siRNA targeting TNF-α in macrophages, reducing pro-inflammatory cytokine expression without significant cytotoxicity. The biodegradability of these nanoparticles ensures minimal accumulation, while their intrinsic zinc ion release can modulate intracellular signaling pathways to enhance transfection efficiency.

subsections.section_title: Wound Healing, Drug Delivery, and Tissue Engineering Applications
subsections.content:
Green-synthesized zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO NPs) have emerged as promising candidates for bone and dental tissue engineering due to their osteoinductive properties, biocompatibility, and ability to enhance mineralization. Studies demonstrate that phytochemically capped ZnO NPs stimulate osteoblast proliferation and upregulate expression of bone-specific markers such as alkaline phosphatase, osteocalcin, and runt-related transcription factor 2 (Runx2). These nanoparticles also promote hydroxyapatite deposition in collagen matrices, mimicking natural bone mineralization processes. In dental applications, ZnO NPs have been incorporated into bioactive scaffolds to enhance dentin remineralization and inhibit cariogenic biofilms without compromising pulp cell viability.

Recent in vitro and in vivo studies have shown that ZnO NPs synthesized using plant extracts significantly improve bone defect healing in rodent models, with enhanced new bone formation and vascular integration compared to controls. Furthermore, their controlled zinc ion release modulates osteoclast activity, maintaining a balanced bone remodeling environment. Functionalization of ZnO NPs with bioactive peptides or polysaccharides has further improved their adhesion to dental tissues and sustained release profiles in oral environments.

subsections.section_title: Wound Healing, Drug Delivery, and Tissue Engineering Applications
subsections.subsection_title: Biofilm disruption and chronic wound management
subsections.content:
Chronic wounds are often complicated by persistent biofilm formation, which impedes healing by shielding pathogens from antibiotics and host immune responses. Green-synthesized zinc oxide nanoparticles (ZnO NPs) have demonstrated potent biofilm-disrupting capabilities due to their ability to penetrate microbial extracellular polymeric substances and induce oxidative stress via zinc ion release and reactive oxygen species generation. Studies have shown that phytochemically capped ZnO NPs effectively inhibit biofilm formation by Staphylococcus aureus and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, two dominant pathogens in chronic diabetic ulcers, at concentrations non-toxic to mammalian cells. The surface chemistry imparted by plant-derived capping agents enhances nanoparticle adhesion to bacterial membranes, promoting membrane disruption and intracellular damage.

Moreover, green ZnO NPs modulate the wound microenvironment by downregulating pro-inflammatory cytokines and promoting macrophage polarization toward the regenerative M2 phenotype, thereby facilitating the transition from chronic inflammation to tissue repair. Recent in vivo models of infected diabetic wounds have reported accelerated wound closure and reduced bacterial load following topical application of biosynthesized ZnO NPs, with histological evidence of re-epithelialization and collagen deposition. These effects are amplified when ZnO NPs are incorporated into hydrogel dressings, enabling sustained release and localized biofilm eradication without systemic toxicity.

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Regulatory Perspectives, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
Reproducibility in green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles remains a persistent challenge due to the inherent variability in biological precursors, including plant extract composition, microbial strain physiology, and environmental growth conditions. Variations in phytochemical profiles—such as flavonoid, alkaloid, or phenolic content—across harvest seasons, geographic origins, or extraction protocols directly influence nucleation kinetics, particle size, and surface capping, leading to inconsistent physicochemical properties between batches. Studies have demonstrated that even minor fluctuations in pH, temperature, or incubation time during biosynthesis can alter ZnO nanoparticle morphology and zeta potential, compromising functional uniformity for biomedical or catalytic applications [1].

Microbial-mediated synthesis introduces additional complexity, as bacterial or fungal metabolic activity is sensitive to culture media composition, growth phase at harvest, and aeration rates, resulting in heterogeneous nanoparticle yields and surface functionalization [2]. These variations are often not fully captured in standard characterization protocols, which typically report average values without quantifying intra-batch dispersion or statistical confidence intervals. Consequently, downstream applications requiring precise dosing, such as targeted drug delivery or antimicrobial coatings, face significant reliability issues [3].

Efforts to standardize protocols have been hampered by the lack of reference materials and metrological benchmarks for green-synthesized nanomaterials. Without certified reference materials or real-time process monitoring, batch-to-batch variability remains largely uncontrolled, limiting industrial scalability and regulatory acceptance [4].

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Regulatory Perspectives, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
The scalability of green-synthesized ZnO nanoparticles remains hindered by the reliance on batch-wise, labor-intensive phyto- or microbial processes that lack process control and automation. Unlike conventional chemical routes, which benefit from established industrial reactors and continuous flow systems, green methods often suffer from low volumetric yields and prolonged reaction times, limiting their economic viability at commercial scales. While some studies report promising yields using fungal or bacterial cultures, the need for sterile conditions, nutrient media, and downstream purification increases operational costs, offsetting the environmental advantages ref [28].

Furthermore, variability in plant biomass composition, seasonal changes in phytochemical content, and inconsistent microbial strain performance introduce significant challenges in maintaining uniform nanoparticle properties across large batches. Efforts to standardize extraction protocols and immobilize biocatalysts have shown partial success, but remain largely confined to laboratory settings ref [28]. Economic analyses comparing green and conventional synthesis routes indicate that while green methods reduce hazardous waste disposal costs, their higher raw material and processing expenses currently make them less competitive for high-volume applications such as coatings or photocatalysis ref [28].

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Regulatory Perspectives, and Future Directions
subsections.content:
The regulatory landscape for green-synthesized zinc oxide (ZnO) nanomaterials remains fragmented, with no globally harmonized safety guidelines tailored to biosynthesized variants. While conventional ZnO nanoparticles are regulated under frameworks such as the EU’s REACH and the U.S. EPA’s TSCA, these lack specific provisions for phytochemical- or microbial-capped nanoparticles, whose surface chemistry and dissolution kinetics differ significantly from chemically synthesized analogues. Recent studies emphasize that capping agents from plant extracts or fungi can alter bioavailability, biodistribution, and toxicity profiles, necessitating revised risk assessment protocols ref [22]. The absence of standardized characterization metrics for green ZnO—such as capping layer thickness, stability in physiological media, and degradation byproducts—further complicates regulatory evaluation.

Emerging efforts by the OECD and WHO have called for tiered testing strategies that account for synthesis origin, yet implementation lags behind innovation. For instance, zebrafish embryotoxicity assays have been proposed as a sensitive in vivo model for green ZnO screening, but their adoption in regulatory pipelines is inconsistent ref [25]. Similarly, long-term in vivo biodistribution data, while available for select biosynthesized formulations, are rarely required for pre-market approval ref [10]. Without mandatory reporting of biosynthesis parameters and capping agent identity, regulatory agencies cannot reliably compare safety profiles across batches or synthesis routes.

Future regulatory frameworks must integrate green synthesis metadata into nanomaterial dossiers and adopt adaptive guidelines informed by real-time toxicokinetic data. Collaborative initiatives between regulatory bodies, green nanotechnology researchers, and industry stakeholders are urgently needed to close this translational gap.

subsections.section_title: Current Challenges, Regulatory Perspectives, and Future Directions
subsections.subsection_title: Emerging trends: AI-assisted design, multifunctional hybrids, and smart responsive systems
subsections.content:
Emerging trends in green ZnO nanomaterials are increasingly driven by AI-assisted design, which accelerates the prediction of optimal synthesis parameters and functional properties by learning from high-dimensional physicochemical datasets. Machine learning models have been employed to correlate phytochemical profiles with nanoparticle size, shape, and bioactivity, enabling rational design without exhaustive trial-and-error experimentation. Concurrently, multifunctional hybrids integrating green-synthesized ZnO with polymers, carbon nanotubes, or magnetic nanoparticles are expanding applications in targeted drug delivery and theranostics. For instance, ZnO-chitosan-graphene oxide composites demonstrate enhanced stability, controlled release, and synergistic antimicrobial effects, as validated in wound healing models. Smart responsive systems, engineered to release Zn²⁺ ions or reactive oxygen species in response to tumor microenvironment cues (e.g., low pH or elevated glutathione), are gaining traction for precision oncology. Such stimuli-responsive behavior has been demonstrated in ZnO@polydopamine core-shell structures that selectively lyse cancer cells while sparing healthy tissue.

Recent advances include AI-guided optimization of ZnO-antibiotic conjugates for overcoming multidrug resistance, where deep learning models predicted synergistic pairings with improved bactericidal efficacy. Additionally, ZnO-based nanosensors functionalized with aptamers and responsive polymers enable real-time monitoring of biomarkers in vivo, exemplified by pH- and enzyme-triggered fluorescence switching in tumor models. These innovations collectively represent a paradigm shift from passive nanomaterials to intelligent, adaptive systems.
